Qxb7 grabbed a free pawn but ignored it — Qd5 lands with real threats down that diagonal, and the shuffling that follows (Qc7, Qd8, Qh7) burns your tempo just holding things together, shrinking your +10.3 by almost four pawns. Ne5 was cleaner: it improves your worst piece first, presses toward d7, and never lets the queen reach d5, so after Qe8 Rc7 Qg8 Nd7+ you're simply steamrolling. When you're crushing, don't grab the free pawn if it opens a diagonal into your own king — finish improving first.

When you're attacking, look for the check that keeps queens on the board, not the first move that simplifies.

drills.coachNote: White's queen on h5 is quietly staring down your rook on e8, and the only thing keeping it safe is your f8 rook backing it up. Rxf4 grabbed the knight with the wrong rook — moving the f8 rook pulls that defender away, so White plays Qxe8+, forking king and rook, and after Kh7 Qe6 you're down a full exchange, turning an equal game into a loss. Qxf4 with the queen does the same job on the knight while keeping both rooks connected, and after Qe2 Rf5 the position stays balanced. Before you capture with a piece, check what it was defending — moving it can hang something two squares away.

drills.coachNote: Look at Black's back rank: the knight on c6 stands directly in front of the rook on d8, and neither is well covered — that's a fork waiting to happen for whichever piece can land there. You played the quiet a4 instead, and Black seized the moment with Nxe5, trading off your centralized knight; after Qxe5 Ne4 you're defending with f3, and your commanding +5.4 shrinks by nearly five pawns. Nxc6 was the shot — capturing the knight and clearing the path so that after Qd6, Nxd8! forks the queen off the rook, and Qxd8 Qxg5 hoovers up an exchange and a pawn besides.
